name: Hassan Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying computer engineering in Munich, which is half electronics and half programming. I live in a student flat with two others, and every morning I cycle in for lectures, then lab work on microcontrollers. On Saturdays I work at a bike shop, not because I need the money but because I like fixing things and the owner, Herr Brandl, pays in coffee and spare parts. I use AI tools now and then, mostly when I'm stuck on a datasheet. My dad has a car garage and my mum is an accountant, and they pay for my studies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected, a bit of a letdown for the people who made predictions. At the bike shop I'd laugh about it with Herr Brandl, who's been saying it's hype since the first chatbot. I'd say it's a decent tool and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine, and my parents' work would stay normal too. My mum does tax returns and my dad repairs cars, and neither is going anywhere fast. I'd still keep an eye on interest rates, since the garage depends on people having cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd finish the first-year exams, keep the Saturday job, and apply for a working-student position at one of the electronics firms near Munich. Those pay decently and count as experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A world where AI is mostly hype is the boring outcome, and I'm okay with boring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned interest rates and the garage. How worried are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You mentioned interest rates and the garage. How worried are you? A little. Dad says the last two years were slow, with people holding their old cars longer, but he has enough regular customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the garage struggled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do if the garage struggled? Help on weekends and cut my own spending. I'd skip the ski trip, which my friends would complain about.

say: I'd say it's about what I **expected**, a letdown for the people who made predictions.
I'd laugh about it with **Herr Brandl** (the bike shop owner).
think: My parents' work, **tax returns** and car repairs, stays normal.
I'd still watch **interest rates** because the garage needs people with cash.
do: Finish first-year exams and keep the **Saturday job**.
Apply for a **working-student** position at an electronics firm near Munich.
Help at Dad's garage on **weekends** if needed.
feel: **Calm**; it's the boring outcome and I'm fine with boring.
S0.quote: A world where AI is mostly hype is the boring outcome, and I'm okay with boring.
fieldNote: Hassan's calm is **family-based**: both parents' work looks safe.
His only worry is the garage's cash flow.
Likes the bike shop for the hands-on feel, not the money.

steps.text: Apply for a working-student job at an electronics firm
Keep the Saturday job at the bike shop
Skip the ski trip if the garage has a slow year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real shift, and it'll help some people and hurt others. I'd say to my course mates that the safe path is to understand how things work underneath, not just to use them. Online I'd probably write a short, boring comment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my mum's job is more exposed than mine. Tax returns, checking and bookkeeping are exactly what the card lists. My own field, with hardware, is slower, but the coding part would be handled by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my mum what her firm is planning and help her learn the new software if she wants. I'd lean my own courses towards embedded systems and power electronics, where there's hardware. And I'd use AI tools more often, in a measured way, to see what they can and can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own plan looks fine, but I'd be watching my mum's office. Being the child who worries about a parent's job feels strange.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your mum's firm doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What is your mum's firm doing? They've started using software to read invoices, and two colleagues left and weren't replaced. She says it's normal, but she's started doing a part-time course in tax law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to her? That I'd help with the course fees if needed, and that she's good with people, which software isn't. She'd say stop worrying, but she'd be pleased.

say: I'd say it's a **real shift** that helps some people and hurts others.
I'd tell course mates to understand how things work **underneath**.
think: My mum's job, **bookkeeping and checking**, is more exposed than mine.
My own field, **hardware**, moves slower, though the coding part will be automated.
do: Ask my mum what her firm plans and help her with new **software**.
Lean towards **embedded systems** and power electronics.
Use AI tools **more often**, in a measured way.
feel: **Uneasy**; strange to be the child worrying about a parent's job.
S1.quote: Being the child who worries about a parent's job feels strange.
fieldNote: The risk he sees is in **his mum's office**, not his own course.
Practical help for his mum shows a steady, helpful nature.
He tries AI more, measured by what it can and can't do.

steps.text: Help my mum test the invoice software her firm uses
Pick embedded systems and power electronics modules
Try an AI tool on one lab task each week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to slow down and find out who's responsible. At home I'd say let's make a plan for the family, because we can't wait for Berlin to sort it out. With friends I'd be a bit grim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried about my mum first, since accounting is thinking work and it would go in the first wave. My dad's garage would last until 2031, but his bookkeeping and ordering would be automated. I'd be graduating into a market with few juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with my parents and add up savings and fixed costs, so we know how long we can hold. I'd ask my mum to look at moving to advice work, and I'd offer to learn the garage's systems. I'd also stay in my course and push for a placement in electronics, because robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd have trouble sleeping, and I'd feel I should be helping instead of studying, but studying is the only helpful thing I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the family talk about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would the family talk about it? My dad doesn't like to say he's worried, so he'd joke about it. My mum would make lists, and I'd probably be the one who says it out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your own savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do with your own savings? I've got about 3,000 euros from the bike shop and gifts. I'd put it in a safe account and not touch it, in case the family needs help.

say: I'd say we need to **slow down** and find out who's responsible.
I'd say at home we must make a **family plan**.
think: My mum's accounting job goes in the **first wave**.
I'd graduate into a market with **few juniors**, and the family would feel it.
do: Sit down with my parents and add up **savings** and fixed costs.
Ask my mum to look at moving into **advice work**.
Push for an **electronics placement**, since robots come later.
feel: **Alarmed**, sleepless, and torn between studying and helping.
S2.quote: I'd feel I should be helping instead of studying, but studying is the only helpful thing I can do.
fieldNote: The alarm comes from his **mum's job**, not his own prospects.
He's the one who says worries out loud in the family.
His 3,000 euros is earmarked as family insurance.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents and add up savings and fixed costs
Put my 3,000 euros into a safe account and leave it
Push for an electronics placement for next summer
Ask Herr Brandl for more Saturday hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a window, and let's use it. I'd say it to my parents and tell them my mum should be learning new skills now, not in 2030. To friends I'd say pick the part of the field machines will need people for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a decent amount of time. I'd graduate in 2029, and my mum could shift jobs before the date. It would still be a tight squeeze, and I'd have to be careful with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree with a focus on embedded systems and power electronics. I'd try for two working-student positions, and I'd work with my mum to find a course she wants. I'd also spend a bit more time with AI tools, since I'd have to use them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but able to cope. It's like carrying a heavy bag for a long walk: you know it's there, but you can still walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your mum should shift jobs. What would you suggest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said your mum should shift jobs. What would you suggest? Something with people, like tax advice for small firms or helping older people with forms. Software is bad at the part where you have to calm someone down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if she refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What if she refused? Then I'd ask her once more and let it be. She's stubborn, and I get that from her.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, so let's use it.
I'd tell my parents Mum should be **learning new skills** now.
think: I'd graduate in **2029**, and Mum could shift jobs before the date.
It would be a **tight squeeze**, and I'd be careful with money.
do: Focus on **embedded systems** and power electronics.
Help my mum choose a **course** she wants.
feel: **Anxious** but able to cope, like carrying a heavy bag on a long walk.
S3.quote: Software is bad at the part where you have to calm someone down.
fieldNote: He treats five years as a **window** for the whole family, not just himself.
Suggests human-facing jobs for his mum, and accepts she may refuse.

steps.text: Take two working-student jobs at electronics firms by 2028
Help my mum pick a tax advice course
Spend an hour a week learning an AI tool
Cut my own spending by a fifth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and most people will treat it as far away. I'd say it to myself too. To friends I'd say good, we can learn things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty okay. My mum would be close to retirement by then, and my dad could sell the garage on good terms. I'd have around seven years of work behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work at a firm near Munich, and learn the AI tools my team uses. I'd save about a fifth of my pay for the first years. And I'd keep fixing bikes, because it keeps my hands busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly calm. A decade feels solid enough to build on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might change your mind about being okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What might change your mind about being okay? If it became clear that firms had started to hire no juniors years ahead. Then I'd have to switch earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting out? Learn the basics deeply, have a hobby with hands, and don't put all your money in one thing.

say: I'd say ten years is long, and most people will treat it as **far away**.
I'd say we can learn things in the **right order**.
think: My mum would be near **retirement** and my dad could sell the garage.
I'd have about **seven years of work** behind me.
do: Finish the degree and work at a **firm** near Munich.
Save a **fifth** of my pay in the first years.
Keep **fixing bikes** to keep my hands busy.
feel: **Uneasy** a little, but mostly calm; a decade feels solid.
S4.quote: Learn the basics deeply, have a hobby with hands, and don't put all your money in one thing.
fieldNote: Ten years lets **retirement** and garage sale line up with the date.
He watches for early signs, like firms hiring no juniors.
Hobby with hands is a theme from the bike shop.

steps.text: Finish the degree and take a job at a Munich firm
Save a fifth of every pay cheque for the first years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my mum's job goes first and I'm still a student. The longer ones let my parents adjust. What would help is retraining that's actually paid for, and help for families where one earner loses work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: One thing. People assume students worry only about themselves, but I'd say a lot of us worry about our parents too.

headlineQuote: People assume students worry only about themselves, but I'd say a lot of us worry about our parents too.
portrait: Hassan is an 18-year-old **computer engineering** student in Munich who works Saturdays at a bike shop.
His parents, a garage owner and an accountant, pay for his studies, so his **cushion is strong**.
He is pragmatic and steady: he tries AI tools when they're proven and thinks in **family** terms.
His fears centre on his **mum's job**, which turns calm worlds into alarm in the fast one.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because his mum's accounting job would go first.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid retraining** and help for families where one earner loses work.
